moves.label: 1. d4
moves.question: What does d4 establish immediately?
moves.message: White occupies d4 and opens the c1 bishop's diagonal. The pawn also controls c5 and e5.
moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: Taking central space can give the pieces more room; that strategic value is separate from an engine verdict.

moves.label: 1... d5
moves.question: How does Black answer White's central occupation?
moves.message: Black meets d4 with a pawn on d5, controlling c4 and e4. Neither side has exchanged its central pawn yet.
moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: A matching central pawn can restrain the opponent's advance without resolving the central tension.

moves.label: 2. Nf3
moves.question: What useful work does the knight do on f3?
moves.message: The knight develops to f3, defending d4 and controlling e5. It will later reach d4 when White begins the manoeuvre against Black's remaining central pawn.
moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: Developing while supporting the centre is a conventional opening principle.

moves.label: 2... Nf6
moves.question: What does Nf6 add to Black's centre?
moves.message: Black's knight supports d5 and controls e4. It also clears g8 for the castling move played on move six.
moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: The knight's development combines central influence with preparation for king safety.

moves.label: 3. c4
moves.question: Why challenge d5 with the c-pawn?
moves.message: c4 attacks Black's d5 pawn while White keeps its own pawn on d4. The two sides now have a concrete central exchange to resolve.
moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: A flank pawn can challenge a central pawn without committing the e-pawn.

moves.label: 3... e6
moves.question: What does e6 defend, and what does it restrict?
moves.message: The e6 pawn defends d5 and opens the f8 bishop's diagonal. It limits the c8 bishop's diagonal, which Black later avoids by developing that bishop to b7.
moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: A solid pawn chain can make a bishop seek a different diagonal.

moves.label: 4. Bg5
moves.question: What is the point of Bg5 in this position?
moves.message: Bg5 attacks the f6 knight along the diagonal to Black's queen on d8. Black's next move, Be7, puts a bishop between the knight and queen.

moves.label: 4... Be7
moves.question: How does Be7 change the pressure on Nf6?
moves.message: The bishop on e7 screens the queen from Bg5 and clears f8 for castling. Bg5 still attacks the knight, but moving it would no longer directly expose the queen.
moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: Breaking a relative pin can be useful even without exchanging the attacking bishop.

moves.label: 5. Nc3
moves.question: What does Nc3 add before the centre is resolved?
moves.message: Nc3 develops the second knight and attacks d5. White now has the c4 pawn and this knight bearing on Black's central pawn.
moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: Several pieces aimed at a central square can make an eventual exchange more consequential.

moves.label: 5... Nbd7

moves.message: e3 defends the d4 pawn and opens the f1 bishop's diagonal. White develops that bishop to b5 before castling.
moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.

moves.label: 6... O-O

moves.message: White advances the h-pawn to h4, where it controls g5. Black's h-pawn is already gone, but the g6 pawn still prevents treating this as an unobstructed passed pawn.
moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: Fixing the opponent's kingside pawns can support later king activity; that strategic inference is separate from the immediate pawn controls.

moves.label: 25... Nc5
moves.question: Where is Black routing the freed knight?
moves.message: Nc5 gives the knight a route to e6. In the actual game, Bf4 is met by Ne6 and both knights are then exchanged.

required_reply_or_cost.text: 26.Bf4 Ne6 27.Nxe6 Kxe6 completes the simplification; Black has not recovered the pawn lost on h6.

moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: Reducing the number of attacking pieces can improve practical defensive chances.

moves.label: 26. Bf4
moves.question: What does the bishop's return to f4 invite?
moves.message: White brings the bishop back toward the centre on f4. Black's Ne6 attacks this bishop and Nd4, but Nxe6 Kxe6 resolves the double attack by trading knights.

required_reply_or_cost.text: 26...Ne6 27.Nxe6 Kxe6 leaves Bf4 on the board and exchanges both knights.

moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: A useful bishop square can still allow the opponent to simplify by attacking another piece at the same time.

moves.label: 26... Ne6
moves.question: What does the double attack by Ne6 achieve?
moves.message: Ne6 attacks both Nd4 and Bf4. White answers Nxe6 Kxe6, keeping the bishop and exchanging both knights while retaining its extra pawn.

required_reply_or_cost.text: 27.Nxe6 Kxe6 is the actual answer; the fork does not win a minor piece.

moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: Black's published defensive aim is to reach an opposite-coloured-bishop ending, not to win a piece with this double attack.

facts.text: Black exchanges Knights to remain with Bishops of {213}opposite colours, which gives him the best chance to draw.

moves.label: 27. Nxe6
moves.question: Does Nxe6 win the knight?
moves.message: White captures Ne6, but Black's Kxe6 recaptures the white knight. Both knights disappear, leaving the bishops and rooks with White still a pawn ahead.

required_reply_or_cost.text: 27...Kxe6 completes the knight trade.

moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: A simplification can preserve a material advantage while removing an active attacking piece.

moves.label: 27... Kxe6
moves.question: Why recapture with the king rather than the f-pawn?
moves.message: Kxe6 completes the knight exchange without moving the f7 pawn. In the book's alternative 27...fxe6, White could place its bishop on e5; that is a comparison line, not what happened.

required_reply_or_cost.text: The actual recapture is Kxe6, preserving Black's f7 and g6 pawns.
Capablanca gives ...fxe6 and Be5 as the hypothetical reason to prefer the king recapture.

moves.uncertainty: The book calls ...fxe6 worse; this baseline checks the stated bishop route but does not independently rank all recaptures.
moves.phase2_general_theory: A king recapture can avoid a pawn-structure concession or an outpost for the opposing bishop.

facts.text: 27...P × Kt would be worse, as White would then be able to post his Bishop at K 5.

moves.label: 28. Rd2
moves.question: What does Rd2 keep under control?
moves.message: Rd2 keeps the rook on the d-file opposite d5 while defending b2 along the second rank. Black next shifts its rook to h8 to attack White's h-pawn.
moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: A rook can combine pressure on an enemy pawn with defence of its own pawns.

moves.label: 28... Rh8
moves.question: Does the attack on h4 win the pawn?
moves.message: Rh8 attacks the h4 pawn, but White answers Rc2 rather than moving the bishop back to defend it. Black returns to c8 and exchanges rooks, so the h4 pawn is never captured in the game.

required_reply_or_cost.text: 29.Rc2 Rc8 30.Rxc8 Bxc8 is the actual continuation; White keeps h4 and its extra pawn.

mistake_responsibility.attribution: Capablanca calls ...Rh8 weak and recommends queenside pawn counterplay.
mistake_responsibility.basis: book commentary after 28...Rh8, page213; phase2 strategic assessment, not engine-verified.

moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: Capablanca calls Rh8 weak and suggests queenside counterplay instead; that strategic verdict is separate from the recorded rook exchange.

facts.text: Black wants to force B - Kt 3. P - K Kt 3 would be bad, on account of P - Q 5; which would get the Black Bishop into the game, even though White could answer P - K 4. The text move is, however, weak, as will soon be seen. His best chance was to play P - Kt 5; and follow it up with P - R 4 and B - R 3. White meanwhile could play P - Kt 4 and R 5, obtaining a passed Pawn, which, with proper play, should win.

moves.label: 29. Rc2
moves.question: How does Rc2 answer a threat on the other wing?
moves.message: White puts the rook on the clear c-file instead of retreating Bf4 to protect h4. After Rc8 Rxc8 Bxc8, both rooks are gone and White still has its extra pawn.

required_reply_or_cost.text: 29...Rc8 30.Rxc8 Bxc8 closes the exchange and preserves the h4 pawn.

moves.uncertainty: The actual rook exchange is established; the result of choosing ...Rxh4 instead is not independently analysed here.
moves.phase2_general_theory: Active counterplay can be more effective than passive defence, but this line alone does not prove every pawn capture by Black fails.

facts.text: Black wants to force B - Kt 3. P - K Kt 3 would be bad, on account of P - Q 5; which would get the Black Bishop into the game, even though White could answer P - K 4. The text move is, however, weak, as will soon be seen. His best chance was to play P - Kt 5; and follow it up with P - R 4 and B - R 3. White meanwhile could play P - Kt 4 and R 5, obtaining a passed Pawn, which, with proper play, should win.

moves.label: 29... Rc8
moves.question: What is the price of returning the rook to c8?
moves.message: Black returns to c8 to contest White's rook on the file. Rxc8 Bxc8 then trades off the last rooks, leaving opposite-coloured bishops and White one pawn ahead.

required_reply_or_cost.text: 30.Rxc8 Bxc8 completes the rook exchange and removes both rooks.

moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: Opposite-coloured bishops can improve drawing chances, but they do not themselves establish a draw.

moves.label: 30. Rxc8
moves.question: What remains after the capture on c8?
moves.message: White captures the last black rook, and Bxc8 immediately trades off White's rook as well. The resulting ending has opposite-coloured bishops with White a pawn ahead.

required_reply_or_cost.text: 30...Bxc8 is essential: Rxc8 is a rook trade, not a rook win.

moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: Removing rooks makes king activity and the pawn structure the main strategic issues.

moves.label: 30... Bxc8
moves.question: What kind of ending does Bxc8 actually leave?
moves.message: Black recaptures the rook with the bishop, leaving only bishops, kings and pawns. The bishops occupy opposite colours, but White still has the extra pawn gained by Bxh6.
moves.uncertainty: The material and bishop colours are directly verifiable; the book's forced-win assessment is not independently proved against all defences.
moves.phase2_general_theory: Capablanca judges this ending won for White; opposite-coloured bishops alone are not enough to decide the result.

facts.text: There are now Bishops of opposite colour, but nevertheless White has an easily-won game. {214}

moves.label: 31. Kf2
moves.question: What does the king's step to f2 prepare?
moves.message: White moves the king to f2 while keeping its bishop active on f4. The actual d4 exd4 sequence then vacates e3, which the king uses on move 33.
moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: Bringing the king into play is a central endgame principle; its best route still depends on the pawn structure.

moves.label: 31... d4
moves.question: What does Black obtain for advancing the isolated pawn?
moves.message: Black gives up the d-pawn to exd4, after which Kd5 blocks and attacks White's new passed pawn. White is then two pawns ahead, so the blockade does not erase the material cost.

required_reply_or_cost.text: 32.exd4 Kd5 is the actual sequence: Black loses its central pawn and places the king in front of White's d4 pawn.

moves.uncertainty: The pawn loss and king blockade are actual events; necessity of ...d4 is only the book's assessment.
moves.phase2_general_theory: Capablanca describes the advance as practically forced to stop White's king entering on either wing; that broader strategic claim is not a verified engine comparison.

facts.text: Practically forced. Otherwise the White King would march up to Q 4 and then to B 5 and win Black's Queen's side Pawns. If Black attempted to stop this by putting his King at Q B 3 then the White King would enter through K 5 into Black's King's side and win just as easily.

moves.label: 32. exd4
moves.question: What does exd4 gain, and what can stop the new pawn?
moves.message: White removes Black's remaining central pawn and becomes two pawns ahead. The pawn on d4 is passed, but Black answers Kd5 to block it and threaten its capture.

required_reply_or_cost.text: 32...Kd5 attacks d4; 33.Ke3 is the played defence of the pawn.

moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: A passed pawn needs support before it can advance safely against an active king.

moves.label: 32... Kd5
moves.question: What does the king attack from d5?
moves.message: Kd5 stands immediately in front of White's passed d4 pawn and attacks it. White replies Ke3, protecting the pawn before Black can take it.

required_reply_or_cost.text: 33.Ke3 defends d4 against a king capture.

moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: A king blockade can restrain a passer, but it also commits the king to that region of the board.

moves.label: 33. Ke3
moves.question: Why is Ke3 important to the passed pawn?
moves.message: Ke3 directly protects d4 against Kxd4. It also keeps White's king close to the pawn as the bishops manoeuvre.
moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: The king and a passed pawn can support one another without the pawn needing to advance immediately.

moves.label: 33... Be6
moves.question: What does the bishop on e6 prepare?
moves.message: Be6 controls d5 and can reach c4 once Black's king leaves d5. The actual Kc6 and a3 sequence clears that route for Bc4+.

required_reply_or_cost.text: 34...Kc6 clears d5; after 35.a3, ...Bc4+ checks the king on d3.

moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: A bishop's checking route can depend on a friendly king first clearing its diagonal.

moves.label: 34. Kd3
moves.question: What does Kd3 keep together?
moves.message: White's king remains immediately behind the passed pawn on d4 and continues to protect it. It will have to answer Bc4+ after Black clears the bishop's route.

required_reply_or_cost.text: 35...Bc4+ 36.Ke3 is the recorded check and response.

moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: Staying close to the passer keeps the pawn secure, even if the king must sometimes change its supporting square.

moves.label: 34... Kc6
moves.question: How does Black keep d5 controlled after leaving it?
moves.message: Black moves the king to c6, where it still controls d5. Be6 also covers d5, and the king's departure opens the bishop's route to c4.
moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: A blockade can be maintained by control of the pawn's next square rather than by occupying that square continuously.

moves.label: 35. a3
moves.question: What does a3 change while the kings wait?
moves.message: White advances a2 to a3, where that pawn controls b4 and is protected by b2. Black uses the next move for Bc4+, so this pawn move does not advance the central passer.

required_reply_or_cost.text: 35...Bc4+ is the actual answer; White retreats the king with 36.Ke3.

moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: A small pawn improvement can be used while maintaining the central pawn's support.

moves.label: 35... Bc4+
moves.question: What does Bc4+ force White to address?
moves.message: The bishop reaches c4 through the now-clear d5 square and checks White's king on d3. White answers Ke3, still protecting the passed pawn on d4.

required_reply_or_cost.text: 36.Ke3 is the actual legal response; the check wins no pawn in this continuation.

moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: A check can displace the king without breaking its ability to defend a pawn.

moves.label: 36. Ke3
moves.question: What is preserved by retreating to e3?
moves.message: White leaves the checked d3 square and returns to e3, continuing to defend d4. Black then restores the bishop to e6 rather than winning the pawn.

required_reply_or_cost.text: 36...Be6 is the actual continuation, with d4 still protected.

moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: A retreat can maintain the essential defensive relationship while conceding a square temporarily.

moves.label: 36... Be6
moves.question: What does the bishop's return to e6 restore?
moves.message: Be6 restores Black's control of d5 after the check on c4. White now changes the bishop's route with Bh6 and Bg7 instead of repeating the previous king manoeuvre.
moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: Breaking a waiting sequence may require improving another piece rather than forcing the king forward immediately.

moves.label: 37. Bh6
moves.question: Why route the bishop through h6?
moves.message: Bh6 prepares Bg7, which White plays on its next turn. From g7 the bishop directly defends White's passed d4 pawn along the g7-f6-e5-d4 diagonal.

required_reply_or_cost.text: 37...Kd5 38.Bg7 is the actual manoeuvre; the supporting diagonal ends at d4.

moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: Capablanca proposes a later Kf4 entry once the bishop supports d4, and contrasts premature g4 with ...f5; neither continuation was played.

facts.text: It is better not to hurry P - K Kt 4 because of P - B 4; for although White could win in any case, it would take longer. Now the White King threatens to help by going in through K B 4 after posting the Bishop {215}at Kt 7, where it not only protects the Q P, but indirectly also the Q Kt P.

moves.label: 37... Kd5
moves.question: Can Kd5 capture the passed pawn now?
moves.message: Black returns the king to d5 in front of the passer. White's king on e3 already protects d4, and the next move Bg7 supplies a second defender from the diagonal.

required_reply_or_cost.text: 38.Bg7 adds bishop protection; ...Kxd4 is not a legal immediate capture while Ke3 defends d4.

moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: Adding a second defender can free the king to work elsewhere without losing the passed pawn.

moves.label: 38. Bg7
moves.question: What does Bg7 complete at the end of the game?
moves.message: Bg7 defends the passed d4 pawn from a distance, allowing White's king to leave its supporting square without abandoning the pawn. Black resigns here, before the king manoeuvre described in the book is played.

required_reply_or_cost.text: The actual game ends after 38.Bg7 with White two pawns ahead and d4 protected by both king and bishop.

moves.uncertainty: The game result is a recorded resignation, not a played-out promotion or an independently established forced-win tree.
moves.phase2_general_theory: Capablanca's intended Kf4 entry exploits the bishop's support of d4; the resignation is factual, while a proof against every defence is beyond this baseline.

facts.text: It is better not to hurry P - K Kt 4 because of P - B 4; for although White could win in any case, it would take longer. Now the White King threatens to help by going in through K B 4 after posting the Bishop {215}at Kt 7, where it not only protects the Q P, but indirectly also the Q Kt P.

The student ought to have realised by this time the enormous importance of playing well every kind of ending. In this game again, practically from the opening, White aimed at nothing but the isolation of Black's Q P. Once he obtained that, he tried for and obtained, fortunately, another advantage of position elsewhere which translated itself into the material advantage of a Pawn. Then by accurate playing in the ending he gradually forced home his advantage. This ending has the merit of having been played against one of the finest players in the world.

moves.label: 1. e4
moves.question: What does e4 open for White?
moves.message: e4 occupies a central square and clears e2 for the queen and f1 bishop. The pawn controls d5 and f5.
moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: A central pawn advance can release pieces as well as claim space.

moves.label: 1... e5
moves.question: How does e5 contest the centre?
moves.message: Black puts its pawn on e5, controlling d4 and f4. This is the pawn White's knight attacks on the next move.
moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: A symmetrical pawn reply can still lead to an asymmetrical piece exchange.

moves.label: 2. Nf3
moves.question: What does the knight attack from f3?
moves.message: Nf3 develops the knight with an attack on e5. Black replies Nf6, counterattacking White's e4 pawn rather than defending e5 directly.

required_reply_or_cost.text: 2...Nf6 attacks e4, setting up the exchange of both e-pawns in the actual game.

moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: Counterattacking an equivalent central pawn is a different way of meeting pressure from adding a defender.

moves.label: 2... Nf6
moves.question: What is Black's answer to the attack on e5?
moves.message: Nf6 attacks the undefended e4 pawn while leaving e5 available to White's knight. The played Nxe5 d6 Nf3 Nxe4 sequence removes both e-pawns and restores equal material.

required_reply_or_cost.text: 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 is the complete central exchange, not a lasting pawn win for either side.

moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: The move order of a counterattack can matter even when the intended final material balance is equal.

moves.label: 3. Nxe5
moves.question: Is Nxe5 a lasting pawn gain?
moves.message: White captures e5, but Black answers d6, drives the knight back and takes e4. Both e-pawns disappear, so White does not retain an extra pawn.

required_reply_or_cost.text: 3...d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 is required to complete the material story.

moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: An opening capture can be one half of a balanced exchange rather than a free gain.

moves.label: 3... d6
moves.question: What does d6 gain before Black takes e4?
moves.message: d6 attacks the knight on e5 and opens the c8 bishop's diagonal. After White retreats Nf3, Black captures e4 to recover the pawn.

required_reply_or_cost.text: 4.Nf3 Nxe4 is the actual response and recovery of material.

moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: Attacking a piece before recovering material can improve the order in which development proceeds.

moves.label: 4. Nf3
moves.question: Why retreat the knight to f3?
moves.message: White withdraws the knight from the d6 pawn's attack. Black then takes e4, leaving both sides without their e-pawns and with equal material.

required_reply_or_cost.text: 4...Nxe4 recovers the pawn Black lost on e5.

moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: A retreat can be an expected part of an opening exchange rather than a loss of material.

moves.label: 4... Nxe4
moves.question: What does Nxe4 restore, and what can attack the knight?
moves.message: Black captures White's e-pawn and restores equal material. White answers Qe2, attacking this knight on the open e-file.

required_reply_or_cost.text: 5.Qe2 creates pressure on Ne4; it does not undo the completed pawn exchange.

moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: An advanced knight can require a careful retreat once the opponent brings a queen to the open file.

moves.label: 5. Qe2
moves.question: How does Qe2 restrict Ne4?
moves.message: Qe2 attacks Ne4 along the open e-file, with Black's king behind it on e8. Black responds Qe7, placing the queen between that knight and king.

required_reply_or_cost.text: 5...Qe7 screens the king and prevents the pin from simply winning Ne4.

moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: A pin can be met by interposing another piece rather than immediately moving the king.

moves.label: 5... Qe7
moves.question: What does Qe7 defend on the e-file?
moves.message: Black places the queen behind Ne4, defending the knight and screening the king from Qe2. White then uses d3 to attack the knight with a pawn, and Black retreats Nf6.

required_reply_or_cost.text: 6.d3 Nf6 is the actual continuation; the knight survives.

moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: An interposition may solve the immediate pin without making the advanced piece a permanent outpost.

moves.label: 6. d3
moves.question: What does d3 ask the e4 knight to do?
moves.message: d3 attacks Ne4 and opens the c1 bishop's route through d2. Black retreats Nf6, and White develops that bishop with Bg5.

required_reply_or_cost.text: 6...Nf6 removes the knight from the pawn attack.

moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: A pawn move can gain time against a piece while releasing one of its own bishops.

moves.label: 6... Nf6
moves.question: What remains after the knight returns to f6?
moves.message: Black saves the knight from d3 and leaves the two queens facing each other on the open e-file. White chooses Bg5 before any queen exchange occurs.
moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: Capablanca's discussion of the next move centres on using development before simplifying.

moves.label: 7. Bg5
moves.question: What does Bg5 develop with a threat?
moves.message: Bg5 develops the bishop and pins Nf6 to the queen on e7. Black chooses Be6 rather than taking White's queen on e2.
moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: Capablanca says a hypothetical ...Qxe2+ Bxe2 would leave Black behind in development; that is a strategic comparison from the book.

facts.text: Played by Morphy, and a very fine move. The point is that should Black exchange Queens he will be a move behind in development and consequently will get a cramped game if White plays accurately.

moves.label: 7... Be6
moves.question: How does Be6 change the queen-exchange option?
moves.message: Be6 develops the c8 bishop onto e6 and places it between the two queens on the e-file. The immediate queen exchange is no longer available while that bishop remains there.
moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: Marshall's preference for developing the bishop over exchanging queens is reported by Capablanca, not independently ranked here.

facts.text: Marshall thought at the time that this was the best move and consequently played it in preference to Q × Q ch.

moves.label: 8. Nc3
moves.question: What central routes does Nc3 provide?
moves.message: White develops the second knight to c3, controlling d5 and e4. The game later uses the d5 jump to attack Black's bishop on e7.
moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: A knight's useful next square can matter more than its present attack count.

moves.label: 8... h6
moves.question: What does h6 make White decide?
moves.message: h6 attacks Bg5. White exchanges that bishop for Nf6 with Bxf6 Qxf6, rather than retreating it.

required_reply_or_cost.text: 9.Bxf6 Qxf6 is a bishop-for-knight exchange; the h-pawn push does not win a piece.

moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: Challenging a bishop can prompt an exchange that changes the remaining minor-piece balance.

moves.label: 9. Bxf6
moves.question: What is exchanged by Bxf6?
moves.message: White captures the f6 knight, but Qxf6 recaptures the bishop. Black retains both bishops while White retains both knights and its f1 bishop.

required_reply_or_cost.text: 9...Qxf6 completes the exchange and keeps Black's pawn structure intact.

moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: Giving up a bishop for a knight can be a deliberate simplification rather than a material gain.

moves.label: 9... Qxf6
moves.question: What does the queen recapture preserve?
moves.message: Qxf6 recovers the bishop without moving Black's f-pawn or doubling its pawns. The queen's later retreat to g7 becomes possible only after the g-pawn advances to g5.
moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: Choosing a queen recapture can preserve the pawns but expose the queen to later attacks.

moves.label: 10. d4
moves.question: What does d4 release as well as occupy?
moves.message: White moves the pawn from d3 to d4, controlling c5 and e5. This also vacates d3 for the f1 bishop, which develops there after Qb5+.
moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: Central space and release of a developing square can be two effects of the same pawn move.

moves.label: 10... Be7
moves.question: What does Be7 make possible?
moves.message: Be7 develops the f8 bishop and clears f8 for kingside castling. White immediately checks with Qb5+, delaying that castling move.

required_reply_or_cost.text: 11.Qb5+ must be answered before Black can castle.

moves.uncertainty: No engine ranking is asserted; the explanation concerns this position and the recorded game.
moves.phase2_general_theory: Completing the path for castling does not mean the king is free to castle on the very next move.

moves.label: 11. Qb5+

facts.text: It is now time to examine the result of the opening. On White's side we find the minor pieces well posted and the Queen out in a somewhat odd place, it is true, but safe from attack and actually attacking a Pawn. {217}White is also ready to Castle. White's position is evidently free from danger and his pieces can easily manœuvre.

On Black's side the first thing we notice is that he has retained both his Bishops, unquestionably an advantage; but on the other hand we find his pieces bunched together too much, and the Queen in danger of being attacked without having any good square to go to. The Bishop at K 2 has no freedom and it blocks the Queen, which, in its turn, blocks the Bishop. Besides, Black cannot Castle on the King's side because Q × P, R - Kt 1; Q - K 4 threatening mate, wins a Pawn. Nor can he Castle on the Queen's side because Q - R 5 would put Black's game in imminent danger, since he cannot play P - R 3 because of B × P; nor can he play K - Kt 1 because of Kt - Kt 5. Consequently we must conclude that the opening is all in White's favour.
